text: If you hold a driver's license, your face is already in a police lineup. You never volunteered for it, and you cannot step out of it.
provenance: If you hold a driver's license, you are in the lineup — a permanent one you never volunteered for and can never step out of.

text: The software takes one image and compares it against millions of driver's license photos and mug shots. People never accused of anything.
provenance: It takes one image and compares it against a vast state database — millions of driver's-license photos and mug shots, ordinary people who have never been accused of anything in their lives.

text: It does not know who anyone is. It returns a ranked list of look-alikes, each scored by a probability. Feed it a blurry photo and it still hands back somebody.
provenance: The software does not know who anyone is. It produces a ranked list of faces that look statistically similar, each one scored by a probability.
Feed it a blurry one, and it will still hand back somebody.

text: You do not have to break a law, know a criminal, or go near a crime scene. To software, you only have to look a little like somebody else.
provenance: You do not have to break a law, know a criminal, or go anywhere near a crime scene. To a piece of software, you only have to look a little like somebody else.

text: Police hand a blurry frame to software and ask it to go find a person.
provenance: So the police did what more and more departments now do by reflex. They handed the blur to software, and they asked it to go find a person.

text: A face on a screen is not supposed to be enough. A match is a lead, not an arrest.

text: In a Detroit suburb, one father was matched to a crime he never heard of. About thirty hours in a cell. He was only in the lineup.
